lessons.title: Conflicting Interests in the British Mandate, c1920–45

before.content_html:
Why Did Britain End Up Running Palestine?

When the First World War broke out in 1914, Palestine was a province of the Ottoman Empire. By 1920 the Ottomans were defeated and Britain held a League of Nations Mandate over the territory. Britain had won the right to govern Palestine, but it had also made three wartime promises that pulled in different directions. The McMahon-Hussein correspondence of 1915–16 had encouraged Sharif Hussein of Mecca to lead an Arab revolt against the Ottomans by hinting at independence for the Arab lands afterwards. The Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 secretly carved up the same Arab lands between Britain and France. The Balfour Declaration of November 1917 then committed Britain to support ‘a national home for the Jewish people’ in Palestine.

Key Fact

Britain made three contradictory wartime promises about the Middle East: McMahon-Hussein (1915–16) to Arab leaders, Sykes-Picot (1916) to France, and the Balfour Declaration (1917) to Zionist leaders. The Mandate over Palestine, awarded in 1920 and confirmed in 1922, locked these promises into one ungovernable territory.

Zionism and the Demand for a Jewish Homeland

Zionism was the political movement, founded by Theodor Herzl in 1897, that argued the Jewish people needed their own state to be safe from antisemitism. Pogroms in the Russian Empire and the Dreyfus Affair in France had convinced Herzl that assimilation in Europe would never protect Jewish communities. The First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897 set Palestine as the target. From the 1880s onwards waves of aliyah brought Jewish immigrants to Palestine. They bought land, drained marshes, founded the city of Tel Aviv in 1909 and built the kibbutz movement — collective farms run on socialist lines. By 1939 the Yishuv — the Jewish community in Palestine — had grown to roughly 450,000 people, around 30 per cent of the population.

Palestinian Arab Nationalism

For the Arab population of Palestine, who in 1920 made up about 90 per cent of inhabitants, the Mandate was experienced as a betrayal. Their leaders had taken Britain’s wartime hints to mean independence. Instead they found Jewish immigration accelerating and land being sold to Zionist settlers, often by absentee landlords living in Beirut or Damascus. Palestinian Arab nationalism developed through institutions such as the Arab Higher Committee under the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini. Riots broke out in 1920, 1921 and 1929, and an open Arab revolt against British rule and Jewish immigration ran from 1936 to 1939. Britain crushed the revolt with around 25,000 troops, but the violence forced policymakers in London to rethink whether the Balfour promise was even achievable.

Top-band answers do not collapse the Mandate dispute into a religious quarrel. The Arab population of Palestine included Christians as well as Muslims, and the conflict was driven by competing nationalisms over the same land. Zionism was a modern political movement responding to European antisemitism; Palestinian Arab nationalism grew out of the wider Arab demand for self-determination after Ottoman rule. Religion mattered — Jerusalem is sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims — but the central question was who would govern, not whose prayers were correct.

Nazi Persecution and the 1939 White Paper

From 1933 the Nazi seizure of power in Germany triggered a new wave of Jewish refugees seeking entry to Palestine. By 1939 around 60,000 had arrived from Germany alone. Arab leaders feared that a continued flow on this scale would soon turn them into a minority in their own country. Faced with the 1936–39 revolt and the prospect of war with Germany, Britain switched policy. The May 1939 White Paper capped Jewish immigration at 75,000 over the next five years — about 1,500 per month — and promised an independent Palestinian state within ten years.

The 1939 White Paper satisfied no one. Arab leaders rejected it because it allowed any further Jewish immigration. Zionists denounced it as a betrayal at the very moment the Holocaust was beginning — David Ben-Gurion famously declared the Yishuv would ‘fight the war as if there were no White Paper, and fight the White Paper as if there were no war’. As news of Nazi extermination camps reached Palestine, Zionist patience with Britain collapsed.

Key Fact

The 1939 White Paper capped Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years (1,500 per month) and promised Palestinian independence in ten years. Arabs rejected it because it permitted any further Jewish immigration. Zionists rejected it as a betrayal during the Holocaust.

1945: The Biltmore Programme and a Britain Out of Options

The 1942 Biltmore Conference in New York — sometimes loosely called the 1945 Zionist conference in exam mark schemes — was a turning point. Until then, mainstream Zionism had pursued a Jewish ‘national home’ that could exist within a British framework. Biltmore demanded an outright Jewish state, unlimited immigration and a Jewish army. By 1945 this position had hardened further: the Holocaust had killed roughly six million European Jews, and the survivors crowded in displaced-persons camps had nowhere to go. Britain emerged from the Second World War economically exhausted, dependent on US loans, and lacking the troops or the will to enforce the 1939 immigration cap. President Truman publicly pressed London to admit 100,000 Holocaust survivors immediately. Britain refused, and Jewish armed groups in Palestine — Haganah, Irgun and Lehi — began a campaign of attacks on British targets that would dominate the next three years.

It is tempting to begin the story in May 1948 when Israel declared independence. Examiner mark schemes for the ‘importance of the end of the Mandate’ question explicitly reward pre-1948 material — the Holocaust, the 1942 Biltmore conference, the Arab fear that Jewish immigration would make them a minority, and Britain’s post-war economic exhaustion. The 1948 war did not start on a blank slate. By 1945 the Yishuv was politically organised, militarily armed and convinced Britain would never deliver a Jewish state. Arab leaders were equally convinced any Jewish state would be imposed on the indigenous majority. Both sides had lost faith in the Mandate years before the British finally walked out.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark ‘Explain the Importance’ question on the end of the Mandate, do not simply describe what the Mandate was. Examiners reward analysis of consequences — how the conflicting promises produced a population in revolt, made British control unworkable and shaped UN involvement after 1945. Pair an immediate consequence (the 1936–39 Arab revolt; the 1939 White Paper) with a longer-term one (the post-1945 collapse of British authority; the path to UN partition). Use specific period vocabulary — Mandate, Yishuv, aliyah, Balfour Declaration — to lift your answer above the threshold band.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the conflicting interests of Jews and Arabs within the British Mandate (c1920–45) for the end of the Mandate in 1948.

lessons.title: The End of the Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–48

before.content_html:
The Yishuv’s Underground Armies, 1945–46

By 1945 the Jewish community in Palestine had three armed groups, each with a different strategy for forcing Britain out. The largest was the Haganah, the official defence force of the Yishuv, which mostly cooperated with British rule but ran an illegal immigration network bringing Holocaust survivors past the Royal Navy blockade. The Irgun, led by Menachem Begin from 1944, broke with the Haganah and adopted open insurgency. The smallest and most extreme group was Lehi, also known as the Stern Gang, which had assassinated the British minister Lord Moyne in Cairo in 1944. After the 1945 Labour government in London refused Truman’s call to admit 100,000 Holocaust survivors, the three groups briefly united in a Jewish Resistance Movement and turned their weapons on British targets.

Key Fact

By 1945 the Yishuv had three armed groups: the Haganah (the mainstream defence force, around 60,000 strong), the Irgun (right-wing insurgents under Menachem Begin) and Lehi/Stern Gang (the smallest and most extreme). Their united campaign of attacks made Britain’s position in Palestine politically unsustainable.

The King David Hotel Bombing, July 1946

The most damaging single attack came on 22 July 1946, when the Irgun bombed the south wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. The hotel housed the headquarters of the British administration and the British army in Palestine. Disguised as Arab workmen, Irgun fighters smuggled milk churns packed with explosives into the basement. Telephone warnings were given but were either ignored, dismissed or did not arrive in time. The blast killed 91 people — British, Arab and Jewish — and injured 46. International reaction was sharp: even mainstream Zionist leaders condemned the attack, and the Haganah formally broke from the operation. The bombing showed the British government two things: insurgent groups could strike at the heart of British rule in Palestine, and holding the Mandate would mean an open-ended counter-insurgency.

Examiners reward students who can analyse what the bombing led to, not just describe what happened. Specific consequences include: the immediate British round-up of around 2,700 Jewish suspects (Operation Agatha and follow-up sweeps); the formal Haganah break from the Irgun; the political shift in London under Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin towards withdrawal; and the loss of British public will to keep paying for a Mandate that was costing about £40 million a year. By February 1947 the cabinet had decided to refer the whole problem to the United Nations.

From Britain to the UN: UNSCOP, 1947

In February 1947 Foreign Secretary Bevin announced that Britain would hand the question of Palestine to the United Nations. The UN set up a special committee, UNSCOP (the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine), with eleven members from neutral countries. The committee toured Palestine in June and July 1947. Its report, published in August, contained two plans: a majority plan recommending partition into a Jewish and an Arab state with an internationalised Jerusalem, and a minority plan for a single federal state. While UNSCOP was working, the British navy intercepted the refugee ship Exodus 1947 and forcibly returned its 4,500 Holocaust survivors to camps in Germany. The image was a public-relations disaster for Britain and pushed undecided UN members towards partition.

UN Resolution 181, 29 November 1947

On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted on the partition plan. Resolution 181 passed by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions. The plan divided Palestine into a Jewish state on about 56 per cent of the land, an Arab state on about 43 per cent, and an internationalised zone around Jerusalem and Bethlehem under UN trusteeship. Both states were to be linked by economic union. Crucially, the Jewish state was awarded territory where Jews were still a minority of the local population, because the plan included the largely empty Negev desert to make the new state economically viable.

Reactions split immediately. Jewish communities in Palestine and around the world celebrated. The Yishuv leadership, including David Ben-Gurion, accepted the plan despite reservations about Jerusalem. Arab leaders — the Arab Higher Committee in Palestine and the Arab League outside it — rejected partition outright. They argued the UN had no right to award the territory of the indigenous majority to a Jewish state, and that the plan gave 56 per cent of the land to a community owning roughly 7 per cent of it.

Key Fact

UN Resolution 181 was passed on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13. It awarded around 56% of Palestine to a Jewish state, 43% to an Arab state, with Jerusalem under international control. Jewish leaders accepted; Arab leaders rejected.

Civil War in Palestine, December 1947 – May 1948

The day after the vote, civil war began. From December 1947 to May 1948 Palestine descended into open fighting between Jewish forces (the Haganah, with the Irgun and Lehi operating alongside) and Palestinian Arab militias supported by volunteer fighters of the Arab Liberation Army. Early Palestinian attacks on supply convoys to Jewish settlements were partly successful, but from March 1948 the Haganah’s Plan Dalet went on the offensive. Towns including Haifa, Tiberias and Jaffa fell to Jewish forces. The most controversial episode was the Deir Yassin attack of 9 April 1948 by Irgun and Lehi forces, in which around 100 Palestinian villagers were killed. News of Deir Yassin spread rapidly and accelerated the flight of Palestinian civilians from areas near the fighting — the beginning of the displacement that Palestinians call the Nakba (‘catastrophe’) and that Israelis remember as part of the War of Independence (covered in detail in Lesson 3).

14 May 1948: The State of Israel is Declared

On 14 May 1948, with the British Mandate set to expire at midnight, David Ben-Gurion read out the Declaration of Independence in the Tel Aviv Museum, founding the State of Israel. The United States recognised the new state within hours. The Soviet Union recognised it three days later. The departure of the British administrator, Sir Alan Cunningham, marked the formal end of the 28-year Mandate. Within hours the armies of Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon would invade.

Examiner indicative content for the ‘importance of the end of the Mandate’ question rewards balanced perspectives. The British government framed the 1948 withdrawal as the only option after the UN had taken responsibility for partition. Critics — both Jewish and Arab — argued that Britain abandoned Palestine without proper transitional arrangements and refused to enforce the partition resolution it had referred to the UN. Strong answers acknowledge that Britain was economically broken (still on rationing, kept solvent by the 1946 American loan) and faced an insurgency it had no political will to defeat — while also recognising that the speed of withdrawal helped trigger the chaos that followed.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Consequence Question, name two distinct consequences and develop each with one or two specific details. Aim for one immediate consequence (e.g. civil war breaking out the next day) and one longer-term consequence (e.g. the Arab states’ invasion that turned civil war into an inter-state war by 14 May 1948). Avoid restating what the event was — that is description, not consequence. The mark scheme awards each consequence separately out of two marks.

before.content_html:
The Five-Front Invasion, May 1948

When the British Mandate ended at midnight on 14–15 May 1948, the regular armies of Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon crossed into the territory of the new state of Israel. Egypt advanced from the south through Gaza and the Negev. Jordan’s British-trained Arab Legion moved into the West Bank and east Jerusalem. Syria attacked from the north-east, Lebanon from the north and Iraqi units operated alongside the Jordanians. On paper the Arab forces outnumbered Israel’s, but they had no unified command, no shared plan and rivalries between the leaders. King Abdullah of Jordan in particular wanted the West Bank for himself rather than for a Palestinian state.

Key Fact

On 15 May 1948 the armies of Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon invaded the new state of Israel. They had numerical advantages on paper but no unified command, conflicting war aims, and were facing a Yishuv that had been preparing for this moment since 1945.

The Phases of the War, May 1948 – January 1949

The war can be divided into clear phases. The first phase from 15 May to 11 June saw heavy fighting and Arab gains, particularly in Jerusalem where the Arab Legion seized the Old City and expelled its Jewish population. A first UN truce ran from 11 June to 8 July, brokered by the UN mediator Count Folke Bernadotte. During the truce Israel re-armed, smuggling weapons in from Czechoslovakia, while the Arab states quarrelled. When fighting resumed in the ‘Ten Days’ from 8–18 July, Israel went on the offensive and captured Lod, Ramle and Nazareth. A second truce held from 19 July to 15 October, although Bernadotte was assassinated by Lehi gunmen in September after he proposed a revised plan giving the Negev to the Arab side.

From October 1948 to January 1949 Israel launched a series of offensives that broke the Arab armies. Operation Yoav drove Egypt out of most of the Negev. Operation Hiram cleared Lebanese and Arab Liberation Army forces from Galilee. Operation Horev pushed Egyptian forces back to the Sinai border. By January 1949 Egypt had agreed to talks. The pattern was clear: the longer the war ran, the more the balance shifted in Israel’s favour as it mobilised its full population, while Arab armies struggled to keep their volunteer or expeditionary forces supplied at distance.

Sources written from each side often present the war as a heroic David-and-Goliath struggle — either Israel against five invading armies, or the Arabs trying to defend Palestine from a well-armed Yishuv. Both pictures contain truth and exaggeration. The Arab armies fielded around 25,000 troops at the outset, while the Yishuv had mobilised the Haganah and was already turning it into the IDF; by the autumn Israel fielded over 100,000 soldiers and was outnumbering its opponents in the field. The new Israeli army also had a unified command, internal lines of communication and a population fighting for its existence. The Arab Legion was professional but small; the other Arab armies were ill-prepared and uncoordinated. Numerical comparisons alone do not explain the outcome.

The Battle for Jerusalem

Jerusalem was the war’s most contested ground. The Arab Legion drove Jewish forces out of the Old City in May 1948, expelling its Jewish population from the Jewish Quarter. West Jerusalem remained in Israeli hands but was nearly cut off — supply convoys had to fight their way along the road from Tel Aviv. The Israelis built the ‘Burma Road’, a hastily improvised track through the Judean hills, to bypass Latrun where Jordanian forces blocked the main route. The fighting ended with the city divided: Jordan held the Old City and east Jerusalem, Israel held the west. This division persisted until 1967.

The 1949 Armistice Agreements

From January to July 1949 Israel signed separate armistice agreements with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. The Egypt agreement was negotiated on the Greek island of Rhodes under UN mediation. Iraq did not sign — its forces simply withdrew. The agreements drew the Green Line, which was treated as the de facto Israeli border until 1967. Crucially, none of the agreements were peace treaties. The Arab states refused to recognise Israel as a permanent neighbour and maintained an economic boycott. The way the war ended therefore guaranteed it would not stay ended.

Key Fact

By the 1949 armistices Israel held about 78% of former Mandate Palestine — around 22% more than the UN partition plan had allocated. Egypt held the Gaza Strip; Jordan held the West Bank and east Jerusalem (formally annexed in 1950).

Territorial Outcome and Two Names for the Same War

The war redrew the map of Palestine. Israel’s share grew from the 56 per cent allocated by Resolution 181 to about 78 per cent. Egypt held the Gaza Strip, where roughly 200,000 Palestinian refugees crowded into a narrow coastal area. Jordan held the West Bank, including east Jerusalem, and formally annexed it in 1950 — an act recognised only by Britain and Pakistan. The Palestinian state envisaged by the UN partition plan was never created. How the war is named reflects how it is remembered: in Israel it is called the War of Independence; among Palestinians it is called the Nakba, meaning ‘catastrophe’. Both labels can appear in good GCSE answers as long as the student treats them as competing names for the same event.

The Refugee Question

Around 700,000 Palestinian Arabs — roughly half the pre-war Arab population — left or were forced from the territory that became Israel. The causes were varied: direct expulsion in some cases (e.g. Lod and Ramle in July 1948), flight from advancing Israeli forces, instruction by Arab commanders to leave temporarily, and panic after the Deir Yassin attack of April 1948. Israeli ‘New Historians’ in the 1980s used newly opened archives to argue that displacement was more systematic than the older Israeli account had admitted — this is named here only as historiographical context, not as a Paper 2 interpretation question. Refugee camps were established in Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, the West Bank and Gaza, run by UNRWA from 1949 (covered in Lesson 4).

Defeat in 1948 destabilised every Arab regime that fought. King Farouk of Egypt was overthrown by the Free Officers in 1952, opening the way for Nasser. Syria saw three military coups in 1949 alone. King Abdullah of Jordan was assassinated at al-Aqsa in 1951 by a Palestinian who blamed him for partitioning Palestine with Israel. The defeat fed pan-Arab nationalism and a generation of officers who believed only revolution at home would deliver victory abroad — a thread that runs straight to Suez 1956 and beyond.

before.description: How Israel built a state, opened its borders to Jewish immigration and lived under cross-border raids.
before.content_html:
A State of Eight Hundred Thousand — and Growing Fast

When the 1949 armistices were signed, Israel was a state of about 800,000 people occupying about 78 per cent of former Mandate Palestine. The new government in Tel Aviv faced three immediate problems at once: securing recognition, mass immigration and constant cross-border raids. The first Prime Minister, David Ben-Gurion, treated all three as connected: a flood of new immigrants would only be safe if the army could defend the borders, and only worth absorbing if the state had the money and recognition to feed them. The decisions taken in this five-year window built the institutions that have shaped Israeli politics ever since.

Building the Israeli Defence Forces

On 26 May 1948, twelve days after independence, Ben-Gurion ordered the dissolution of the Yishuv’s separate armed groups and the creation of a single national army — the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF). The Haganah formed the core; the Irgun and Lehi were forcibly absorbed, sometimes by force of arms (the Altalena affair in June 1948 saw the Irgun’s last separate weapons shipment shelled by Haganah artillery off Tel Aviv beach). From 1949 the IDF introduced compulsory conscription for almost all young men and women, making the army the single most important national institution. By the mid-1950s every Israeli citizen would either serve in the IDF or know somebody who had.

Key Fact

The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) were created on 26 May 1948 from the Haganah, with the Irgun and Lehi forcibly absorbed. Compulsory conscription from 1949 made the IDF the central institution of the Israeli state.

The Law of Return, 1950

In July 1950 the Knesset passed the Law of Return, granting any Jew anywhere in the world the right to immigrate to Israel and acquire citizenship. The law was both a moral statement after the Holocaust and a practical demographic strategy. Between 1948 and 1951 about 700,000 Jewish immigrants arrived — roughly equal to the entire Yishuv before independence. Around half were Holocaust survivors from displaced-persons camps in Europe; the other half were Jews from Arab and Muslim countries (Yemen, Iraq, Morocco, Egypt and elsewhere) where their position became dangerous after 1948. By the end of 1951 Israel’s population had roughly doubled.

Absorbing this wave was painful. Immigrants were housed in tent cities and tin-shack ma’abarot; food was rationed for years; Jews from Arab countries faced discrimination from European-born Israelis (the Ashkenazi-Mizrahi divide that still shapes Israeli politics). But the demographic effect was decisive: Israel could now field a large army from a Jewish majority population and could not realistically be reversed by an Arab military victory short of total war.

A common Israeli argument is that, just as Israel absorbed Jewish refugees from Arab countries, the Arab states should have absorbed the Palestinian refugees. The Palestinian counter-argument is that the two cases are not comparable: Jewish immigrants came to a state that defined itself as their national home, while Palestinian refugees were displaced from their own land and want to return to it. Most Arab states refused full citizenship to Palestinian refugees on the grounds that absorption would extinguish the right of return. Jordan was the exception, granting citizenship to Palestinians on the West Bank and east Jerusalem after annexation. The argument has been live since 1949 — and is one reason mark schemes reward students who hold multiple perspectives at once.

UNRWA and the Refugee Camps

The UN General Assembly created UNRWA in December 1949 to feed, school and shelter the roughly 700,000 Palestinian refugees from the 1948–49 war. UNRWA established camps in the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. The camps were intended as temporary, but by 1955 they had become semi-permanent towns with schools, clinics and dense populations of stateless people. Israel refused to allow refugees to return; the Arab states (with the partial exception of Jordan) refused to grant them citizenship. The camps therefore became a long-term political reality: a young, educated and stateless population that would supply recruits to fedayeen raiders in the 1950s and to the PLO from 1964.

US Aid and Diplomatic Recognition

President Truman’s recognition of Israel within hours of the 14 May 1948 declaration set a pattern of US support, although early aid was modest. Between 1949 and 1955 Washington provided around $290 million in loans and grants — significant for a small new state but smaller than the aid the US would later give. The US balanced support for Israel with concern for its oil interests and Cold War alliances in the Arab world. The Soviet Union had been the second country to recognise Israel and supplied weapons via Czechoslovakia during the 1948 war, but Stalin turned hostile by 1950 as Israel aligned with the Western camp. By 1955 the US-Soviet pattern that would shape the wars of 1956, 1967 and 1973 was already setting hard.

The Border War: Fedayeen Raids and Israeli Reprisals

The 1949 armistice borders ran through villages and farmland; thousands of Palestinians lived just yards from the homes they had lost. From 1949 onwards small groups of fedayeen — armed Palestinians, sometimes acting independently, sometimes sponsored by Egyptian or Jordanian intelligence — crossed the lines to attack Israeli farms, settlements and roads. The IDF developed a doctrine of disproportionate reprisal raids: respond to any cross-border attack with force several times greater, against the territory the raiders came from. Two reprisals especially stand out.

The Qibya raid of October 1953, on a Jordanian-controlled West Bank village, was carried out by Unit 101 under a young officer named Ariel Sharon. Around 69 Palestinian villagers, more than half of them women and children, were killed when houses were demolished with their inhabitants inside. The UN Security Council condemned Israel; the raid did not stop fedayeen attacks, but it did establish reprisal as the Israeli norm. The Gaza raid of February 1955, in which an IDF parachute battalion killed 38 Egyptian soldiers in a raid on an Egyptian army base, marked a turning point in Israel’s relations with Egypt. Nasser, only recently in power, treated the raid as a national humiliation and accelerated the Egyptian arms purchase from Czechoslovakia in 1955 that helped trigger the Suez Crisis (covered in Lesson 5).

Key Fact

Two IDF reprisal raids defined the early 1950s: Qibya (October 1953, in Jordanian-controlled West Bank, around 69 villagers killed) and Gaza (February 1955, 38 Egyptian soldiers killed). Together they hardened the Egyptian-Israeli relationship and pushed Nasser towards Soviet weapons.

A summer 2024 Q2 narrative asked specifically about ‘relations between Israel and Egypt 1949–56’. The lesson’s spine of fedayeen raids, the 1955 Gaza reprisal and Nasser’s Czech arms deal answers that prompt directly. Strong narratives connect events causally: armistice without peace treaty creates the border problem; Palestinian refugees in Gaza supply fedayeen recruits; Israeli reprisal in February 1955 gives Nasser a reason to rearm with Soviet weapons; Egyptian rearmament gives Israel a reason to plan a pre-emptive war. By 1956 the components of the Suez Crisis are all in place.

lessons.title: Suez 1956 and the Arab Nationalist Surge

before.content_html:
From the Free Officers to Nasser’s Egypt

In July 1952 a group of young army officers, calling themselves the Free Officers, overthrew King Farouk of Egypt. Farouk had been discredited by Egypt’s defeat in the 1948–49 war with Israel, by corruption at court, and by the continued British military presence at the Suez Canal Zone. Within two years one of the conspirators, Gamal Abdel Nasser, had pushed his fellow officers aside and emerged as Egypt’s undisputed ruler. By 1956 Nasser was using the radio station Voice of the Arabs to broadcast a vision of pan-Arabism to households from Casablanca to Baghdad: one Arab nation, free of British and French control, hostile to Israel and aligned with neither superpower bloc.

Key Fact

The Free Officers’ coup of July 1952 ended the monarchy of King Farouk; Nasser emerged as Egypt’s leader by 1954 and used radio propaganda to position himself as the champion of Arab nationalism against British, French and Israeli power.

The Czech Arms Deal, September 1955

Nasser’s first major Cold War move grew out of the Israeli reprisal raid on Gaza in February 1955, which had killed 38 Egyptian soldiers. Refused modern Western weapons by the United States and Britain (who feared upsetting Israel), Nasser turned to the Soviet bloc. In September 1955 he announced an arms purchase from Czechoslovakia: hundreds of tanks, jet fighters and bombers, paid for in cotton. The deal broke the Western monopoly on supplying weapons to the Middle East and brought Soviet equipment into Egyptian hands for the first time. The Eisenhower administration was alarmed and, in retaliation, withdrew its offer to fund the Aswan High Dam in July 1956. Nasser responded a week later.

Nationalisation of the Suez Canal, 26 July 1956

In a speech in Alexandria, Nasser announced that Egypt was nationalising the Suez Canal Company — the Anglo-French firm that had run the canal since 1869. Tolls would now go to Egypt and would, he said, fund the Aswan Dam. The Canal carried roughly two thirds of Western Europe’s oil and was widely treated as a strategic British and French asset; nationalisation was therefore experienced in London and Paris as both an economic and a colonial humiliation. Prime Minister Anthony Eden compared Nasser to Hitler in private; the French government wanted Nasser removed both for Suez and for his support of the Algerian rebels then fighting France.

Many British contemporaries claimed Nasser had stolen private property. In fact Egypt offered to compensate the shareholders at the Paris stock-exchange price and pledged that international shipping could continue using the Canal. International lawyers, including in the United States, judged the act lawful: a sovereign state had the right to nationalise companies on its territory provided compensation was paid. The British and French response was therefore a political and military choice rather than a legal necessity — a point examiners reward when students place the events in their Cold War and decolonisation context, not just inside a moral frame.

The Sèvres Protocol

Through the autumn of 1956, Britain, France and Israel held secret talks at Sèvres outside Paris. The resulting Sèvres Protocol set out a deception: Israel would invade Sinai; Britain and France would issue an ultimatum demanding both sides withdraw ten miles from the Canal; Egypt would refuse; Britain and France would ‘intervene to protect international shipping’ and seize the Canal Zone. Israel had its own reasons — ending fedayeen raids from Gaza, reopening the Straits of Tiran for shipping to Eilat and degrading Nasser’s new Soviet weapons before they were absorbed.

War, 29 October – 7 November 1956

Israeli paratroopers dropped into the Mitla Pass on 29 October. The IDF advanced quickly through Sinai. The Anglo-French ultimatum was issued and rejected as planned, and on 5–6 November British and French paratroopers and marines landed at Port Said. Militarily the operation succeeded: the Canal Zone was within reach. Politically it collapsed. The United States, kept in the dark, was furious. President Eisenhower refused to support sterling on the foreign-exchange markets, ordering the IMF to block any British application for emergency loans; the Bank of England was within days of having to devalue. The Soviet Union threatened nuclear action against London and Paris (almost certainly a bluff, but a frightening one in 1956). Eden ordered a ceasefire on 7 November; British, French and Israeli forces withdrew from Egyptian territory by March 1957.

Key Fact

The Suez intervention failed because the United States used economic pressure on the pound sterling to force a British ceasefire and the Soviet Union threatened military action. By March 1957 all three invading forces had withdrawn from Egyptian territory.

Outcomes: A Humiliation That Became a Victory

For Egypt, defeat on the battlefield turned into political triumph. Nasser kept the Canal, kept his army in place and was acclaimed across the Arab world as the man who had faced down two old colonial powers and survived. UNEF, the first UN peacekeeping force, was deployed along the Egypt-Israel border, freezing the Sinai front for a decade. For Britain and France the crisis confirmed that the era of independent Anglo-French military action east of Suez was over. Eden resigned in January 1957. For Israel the war was a tactical success but a strategic stalemate — Sinai was handed back, but the Straits of Tiran were now open and fedayeen raids subsided. For the United States, Eisenhower set a marker: Washington would oppose old-style colonial intervention in the Middle East, and would prefer to deal directly with Arab governments itself.

The United Arab Republic, 1958

Nasser’s prestige peaked in February 1958 when Syria, fearing a communist takeover at home, asked to merge with Egypt. The two countries formed the United Arab Republic (UAR), with Nasser as its president and Cairo as its capital. To pan-Arab opinion the UAR seemed to be the first step towards a single Arab state stretching from the Atlantic to the Persian Gulf. The reality was more difficult. Egyptian officials ran the Syrian provinces; Syrian businessmen and army officers resented Cairo’s dominance; the union dissolved in September 1961 when Syrian officers staged a coup. The UAR collapsed but its symbolic effect endured — pan-Arabism had become the leading ideology of the region, and Nasser the leading Arab.

Indicative content for ‘importance of the Suez Crisis for Egypt’s leadership of the Arab world’ rewards downstream consequences rather than narrative. Strong answers connect Suez to (i) Nasser’s personal prestige and Voice of the Arabs broadcasting reach; (ii) the UAR of 1958 as the most concrete expression of his pan-Arab claim; (iii) the confidence that fed into the road to 1967, with Arab states deferring to Cairo on Israel policy. Weaker answers describe the canal nationalisation and stop there. The lesson’s spine — humiliation that became victory, leading to political union — is exactly the chain examiners want.

lessons.title: Road to the Six Day War, 1964–67

before.content_html:
A Region Calmer on the Surface

By 1964 the Sinai front had been quiet for eight years. UNEF still patrolled the Egypt-Israel border under the agreement that ended the Suez Crisis. Israel had used the years of relative peace to build its army, develop its agriculture and divert water from the Sea of Galilee through the National Water Carrier. Yet the underlying disputes had not been resolved: no Arab state recognised Israel; the Palestinian refugees remained in camps; the Straits of Tiran were technically open but politically contested. By 1967 a chain of small decisions, miscalculations and pieces of bad intelligence would turn three years of fragile calm into the most decisive war of the conflict.

The Cairo Conference and the Founding of the PLO, 1964

In January 1964 the first Cairo Conference brought thirteen Arab heads of state together. Two decisions shaped the years that followed. First, the conference agreed a coordinated response to Israel’s National Water Carrier — a plan, eventually unworkable, to divert the headwaters of the Jordan before they reached Israel. Second, Nasser sponsored the founding of the PLO — the Palestine Liberation Organisation — as an umbrella body intended to keep the Palestinian cause under Cairo’s control. From the start the PLO had a rival: Fatah, founded by Yasser Arafat in 1959, which believed that only armed Palestinian action would force the issue and was unwilling to be an Egyptian instrument.

Key Fact

The 1964 Cairo Conference founded the PLO under Egyptian sponsorship to control the Palestinian cause. Yasser Arafat’s Fatah, founded in 1959, refused to wait for Arab state action and pushed independent guerrilla raids on Israel from 1965, sponsored increasingly by Syria.

Fatah Raids and the Samu Reprisal, November 1966

From 1965 Fatah raids into Israel grew in number. Most originated in Syria, whose new Ba’athist government treated confrontation with Israel as core ideology, but the fighters often crossed into Israel through Jordan because the Jordanian-Israeli border was easier to cross unobserved. After a Fatah landmine killed three Israeli soldiers in November 1966, the IDF retaliated — not against Syria, but against the West Bank village of Samu. Israeli troops destroyed about 125 houses and killed sixteen Jordanian soldiers and three civilians. King Hussein of Jordan was humiliated; Palestinians on the West Bank rioted because Hussein had failed to defend them; Egypt was accused by other Arab states of hiding behind UNEF rather than confronting Israel. The raid against Hussein had pushed all three Arab front-line states closer to a confrontation Egypt had been trying to avoid.

The Air Battle of 7 April 1967

In April 1967 a long-running argument over Israel-Syria water rights along the Sea of Galilee turned into open shooting. On 7 April Israeli jets engaged Syrian aircraft over the Golan Heights and shot down six Syrian MiGs, two of them in dogfights over Damascus itself. The episode was a humiliation for Syria and a warning that Israel could strike inside Syrian airspace at will. Cairo radio still broadcast confidence; in private, Egyptian generals were uneasy about being dragged into a war their army was not yet ready to fight.

Soviet Misinformation, May 1967

In mid-May the Soviet Union told Egypt that Israel was massing eleven to thirteen brigades on the Syrian border ready to invade. The information was wrong — Israeli officials offered to take Egyptian or Soviet observers to the border to prove there were no troops there — but Nasser had to act on it. He could not let pan-Arab opinion accuse him of abandoning Syria. On 14 May 1967 Egyptian troops moved into Sinai. On 18 May Nasser asked the UN to remove UNEF; Secretary-General U Thant agreed, and the buffer that had kept the peace since 1956 disappeared within hours.

Many narratives reduce the road to 1967 to Nasser’s aggression. The fuller picture is that Cairo was responding to Soviet intelligence it could not verify, to pressure from Damascus to back the Ba’athists after the air battle of 7 April, and to a domestic audience that expected him to lead the Arab world against Israel. He removed UNEF and closed the Straits of Tiran in May 1967 partly to bluff Israel into accepting Egyptian deterrence; he did not expect Israel to strike first. Israeli decision-makers, for their part, treated his moves as a casus belli even though there is no documentary evidence that Egypt planned to invade. Cold War alignments — Soviet support for Egypt and Syria, US tilt towards Israel — turned a regional spiral into a flashpoint with global stakes.

Closure of the Straits of Tiran, 22 May 1967

On 22 May Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping — cutting off the Israeli port of Eilat from oil deliveries. Israel had said publicly since 1957 that closure of the Straits would be a casus belli — an act justifying war. Diplomats in Washington and London tried to assemble an international flotilla to reopen the Straits, but the effort got no further than meetings. From 22 May to 5 June, Israel had two weeks in which to decide whether to strike first.

Indicative content for the closure of the Straits expects two distinct consequences pitched at different time horizons. The strongest pair is (i) immediate — the Israeli cabinet treated closure as a casus belli, accelerating the decision to launch a pre-emptive strike within fourteen days; (ii) longer-term — closure escalated Arab confidence and pulled Jordan into the 30 May mutual defence pact, which made the West Bank a battlefield in June and produced the second wave of Palestinian refugees. Weaker answers offer two near-identical ‘Israel wanted to fight’ points; the question rewards different effects, not the same effect twice.

Mutual Defence Pacts and the View from Washington and Moscow

On 30 May King Hussein of Jordan flew to Cairo and signed an Egyptian-Jordanian mutual defence pact, accepting Egyptian command of Jordanian forces in any war. Iraq joined a few days later. To Israeli planners the encirclement was now physical: Egyptian forces in Sinai, Syrian guns on the Golan, Jordanian artillery within range of Tel Aviv. The Johnson administration in Washington warned Israel privately not to strike first; the Soviet Union sent similar warnings to Egypt to avoid being the aggressor. Both superpowers, distracted by Vietnam and Berlin, hoped a diplomatic solution could be found in time. Neither succeeded. By the night of 4 June Israel’s cabinet had voted for war; the strike came at dawn on 5 June.

Key Fact

Four decisions made war almost inevitable: Egyptian troops moved into Sinai on 14 May 1967; UNEF was withdrawn at Egypt’s request on 18 May; the Straits of Tiran were closed on 22 May; and on 30 May Jordan signed a mutual defence pact placing its army under Egyptian command.

Examiners reward precise dates and a clear ‘this in turn’ chain.

lessons.title: The Six Day War and Its Aftermath, June 1967

before.content_html:
A Pre-emptive Strike at Dawn

At 7.45am on 5 June 1967 the Israeli Air Force took off in waves and flew low over the Mediterranean to avoid Egyptian radar. Within three hours about 300 Egyptian aircraft had been destroyed on the ground at airfields across Sinai and the Nile Delta. The pre-emptive strike gave Israel air supremacy on every front from the first morning of the war and made the ground campaign that followed possible. Egypt and Syria announced false victories on the radio for two days; on the ground, Israel was already winning.

Key Fact

On the morning of 5 June 1967 the Israeli Air Force destroyed about 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground in three hours. Air supremacy on the first day made the rapid Israeli ground victories on every front possible.

The Three Fronts

On the southern front the IDF’s armour pushed across Sinai to the Suez Canal in four days, breaking the Egyptian army at Bir Lahfan and Mitla Pass. On the eastern front Jordan, bound by its 30 May pact with Egypt, opened artillery fire on Jewish West Jerusalem on 5 June. Israel responded by overrunning the West Bank and East Jerusalem in three days; Israeli paratroopers reached the Western Wall on 7 June for the first time since 1948. On the northern front Israeli forces stormed the Golan Heights on 9–10 June, displacing Syrian artillery that had shelled Israeli farms below for years. By 10 June a UN-brokered ceasefire was in force on every front.

Casualties and the Map of June 11th

Israeli casualties were roughly 800 dead and 2,500 wounded; Arab casualties were perhaps 18,000 to 20,000 dead, with much greater wounded and prisoner figures. Israel had quadrupled the territory it controlled. From Egypt it now held Sinai and the Gaza Strip; from Jordan, the West Bank and East Jerusalem; from Syria, the Golan Heights. These four territories — together known as the Occupied Territories — framed the politics of the conflict for the next half-century. East Jerusalem was annexed by Israel within weeks; the others were placed under military government, with Jewish settlement programmes beginning in the West Bank and Golan within months.

The Second Wave of Palestinian Refugees

Between 280,000 and 325,000 Palestinians fled the West Bank into Jordan during and after the war. Some had been refugees from 1948 and were now displaced for a second time. Jordan’s population swelled overnight, and the refugee camps in the East Bank filled with younger, more militant residents who would shape Black September three years later. Inside the West Bank, the Palestinians who remained came under Israeli military rule for the first time. Arabic-speaking communities in East Jerusalem found themselves residents of a unilaterally annexed Israeli capital, with restricted political rights compared to Israeli Jews.

Some students argue that the Six Day War settled Israel’s borders. The opposite is closer to the truth: the war replaced the relatively short 1949 armistice lines with much longer borders running through hostile populations, and the unresolved status of the Occupied Territories has driven every conflict since — the Yom Kippur War of 1973, the Lebanon invasion of 1982, the First Intifada from 1987 and the Oslo era after 1993. Israel’s gain of strategic depth was real; its gain of strategic security was not. Examiners reward students who treat 1967 as the start of an occupation problem, not the end of a conflict.

UN Resolution 242, 22 November 1967

After months of negotiation the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 242. It set out the land for peace principle: Israel should withdraw from territory occupied in the recent conflict in exchange for Arab recognition of Israel’s right to exist within secure and recognised boundaries. The English text said ‘territories’ rather than ‘the territories’, an ambiguity Israel cited to argue that withdrawal need not be from all the land. The French text said ‘des territoires’, which Arab governments and most international lawyers read as meaning all of them. The same words have been the basis for every peace process since — Camp David, Oslo, the road map, all begin with Resolution 242.

A strong importance answer on Resolution 242 explains why the wording dispute mattered, not just that it existed. Israeli governments cited the indefinite article in the English text to argue that withdrawal need not be total — specifically that Sinai could be returned without giving up the West Bank or Golan. Arab governments and the French and Russian texts said the opposite. The ambiguity meant 242 produced no immediate withdrawal but it also made every later negotiation possible: each side could come to the table without conceding territory in advance. Camp David in 1978 implemented 242 for Sinai; Oslo in 1993 used 242’s language for the Palestinian track. The resolution’s usefulness was in what it left open, not in what it settled.

The Khartoum Three Nos and the Closed Canal

In September 1967 the Arab League met at Khartoum and issued what became known as the Khartoum Resolution — the ‘three nos’: no peace with Israel, no recognition, no negotiation. The resolution closed off the diplomatic route Resolution 242 had opened, at least for the moment. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait agreed to subsidise Egypt and Jordan instead of pressing them to negotiate. The Suez Canal, blocked by sunken ships during the war and now front-line territory, stayed closed to all shipping until 1975 — one of the global economic consequences of 1967.

Key Fact

UN Resolution 242 (22 November 1967) set out the land for peace principle as the basis for ending the conflict. The Khartoum Resolution of September 1967, with its ‘three nos’ — no peace, no recognition, no negotiation — closed off the immediate diplomatic route, but 242 remained the framework for every later negotiation.

The Superpower Aftermath

The war reshaped Cold War alignments in the region. The Soviet Union broke off diplomatic relations with Israel and accelerated the rearmament of Egypt and Syria, sending in Soviet advisers and surface-to-air missile crews. The United States, which had stayed officially neutral during the war, now tilted decisively towards Israel as a Cold War ally; aid figures rose sharply from 1968 onwards. France, traditionally Israel’s arms supplier, broke with Israel under President de Gaulle and became an arms supplier to Arab states instead. The diplomatic positions hardened by 1967 framed every later war and every later negotiation, including the Yom Kippur War of 1973 and the shuttle diplomacy that followed.

lessons.title: Terrorism, the War of Attrition and Yom Kippur, 1967–73

before.content_html:
After 1967: A Stalemate Both Sides Tried to Break

The defeat of June 1967 left Egypt without Sinai, Jordan without the West Bank and Syria without the Golan, and the ‘three nos’ of Khartoum left no diplomatic route to recover them. Each side tried different tools to break the stalemate. Egypt under Nasser fought a low-intensity war along the Suez Canal. Palestinian groups switched to international terrorism to force the world to notice the cause. Sadat, after Nasser’s death in 1970, prepared a limited war designed to make negotiation politically possible. The years 1967–73 ended the post-1967 freeze and set up the diplomacy of the late 1970s.

The War of Attrition, 1969–70

From March 1969 to August 1970 Egypt fought a War of Attrition against Israeli forces along the eastern bank of the Suez Canal. Egyptian artillery hammered Israeli positions; Israeli aircraft struck deep inside Egypt; the Soviet Union sent in surface-to-air missile crews and pilots, drawing the superpowers very close to direct contact. About 1,400 Israeli and 5,000 Egyptian soldiers died over eighteen months. The war ended in a US-brokered ceasefire on 7 August 1970. It produced no territorial change but it taught Sadat, who succeeded Nasser in September 1970, that pure attrition would not move Israel; only a war that threatened to escalate to the superpowers could do that.

PFLP Hijackings: Dawson’s Field, September 1970

In early September 1970 the PFLP — the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine — hijacked four civil airliners on the same day, flew three of them to a desert strip in Jordan they renamed Revolution Airport (the British called it Dawson’s Field) and held more than 300 hostages for ten days. The PFLP’s aim was political theatre: to force Western governments to release Palestinian prisoners and to put the Palestinian cause on every front page in the world. Most hostages were released; the aircraft were blown up in front of news cameras. The hijackings became the most-watched televised act of political violence to date and gave international air travel a new permanent feature: passenger and luggage screening.

Key Fact

The PFLP hijackings of September 1970 took four civil airliners to Dawson’s Field in Jordan and held more than 300 hostages. The challenge to King Hussein’s authority on his own soil triggered the Jordanian army’s assault on the PLO and the expulsion known as Black September.

Black September, 1970

By September 1970 the PLO and its associated factions had effectively built a state within a state in Jordan: armed checkpoints, refugee-camp courts, taxes on Palestinian businesses. King Hussein decided that the PFLP hijackings on Jordanian soil were a direct challenge he could no longer survive. On 17 September the Jordanian army moved against PLO bases in Amman and the camps. Fighting lasted ten days and killed several thousand Palestinians; Syria briefly intervened with tanks before withdrawing under Israeli pressure. By July 1971 the last PLO fighters had been pushed out of Jordan into Lebanon. Palestinians remembered September 1970 as Black September — and the militant group that took the same name carried it forward into the 1972 Munich Olympics.

Munich Olympics, September 1972

On 5 September 1972 eight members of the Black September Organisation entered the Israeli compound at the Munich Olympic Village, killed two Israeli athletes and took nine hostages. A botched West German rescue attempt at Fürstenfeldbruck airfield ended with all nine hostages, five of the eight attackers and one police officer dead. The attack was watched live by an estimated 900 million people. For the Palestinian movement it produced a publicity bonanza followed by an enormous political price: most Western opinion turned against terrorism as a tactic, and Israeli intelligence launched ‘Operation Wrath of God’, a long campaign of targeted killings against those it judged responsible. International attitudes towards the Palestinian cause hardened in the short term, even as the cause itself became impossible to ignore in any later peace process.

A common misconception is that hijackings and Munich strengthened Palestinian sympathy. The 2022 Q3 examiner exemplar shows top-band answers analysing both effects at once: visibility went up, sympathy went down, and crucially Palestinian leaders lost their base in Jordan. The same logic applied at Munich: the cause became globally famous and globally toxic in the same moment. By 1974 Arafat himself was distancing the PLO from international terrorism — and his UN speech that November used the line ‘I have come bearing an olive branch and a freedom fighter’s gun’ precisely to manage that mixed legacy.

Sadat, the Soviets and Settlement Building

Anwar Sadat succeeded Nasser in September 1970 with a plan few in Cairo or Washington took seriously. In July 1972 he expelled around 20,000 Soviet military advisers, the move Henry Kissinger only later realised had cleared the way diplomatically for the United States to broker a postwar settlement in which Egypt could not be accused of being a Soviet client. Inside the Occupied Territories, Israeli policy was hardening. From 1968 Israeli governments authorised the first Jewish settlements in the West Bank (Kfar Etzion) and Golan; settlement-building became a normalised state policy under both Labor and Likud governments. The negotiating space was shrinking even as Sadat was preparing to force one open.

The Yom Kippur War, October 1973

On 6 October 1973, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal under air-defence cover and Syrian forces stormed the Golan Heights. Israeli intelligence had detected the build-up but the Cabinet, like its allies in Washington, had assumed Sadat would not actually attack. The first ten days of the Yom Kippur War were the worst military shock Israel had experienced since 1948. Settlements on the Golan came under direct attack; Israeli reservists were rushed to the front; tank battles in the Sinai were the largest of any conflict since the Second World War. The United States organised a major airlift of weapons (Operation Nickel Grass) on 14 October. By 22 October Israel had pushed back, encircled the Egyptian Third Army on the west bank of the Canal and was within striking distance of Damascus.

Resolution 338 and the Settlements That Followed

A US-Soviet brush with confrontation forced both superpowers to push for a ceasefire. Resolution 338 on 22 October called for an immediate ceasefire and the implementation of Resolution 242 — reactivating the land for peace principle for the first time since Khartoum. The Egyptian Third Army was rescued from encirclement by US diplomatic pressure on Israel; Sadat had achieved his political objective — restoring Egyptian honour and forcing the United States to mediate — even though Egypt had been militarily outflanked by the war’s end. Inside the Occupied Territories, Israeli settlement-building accelerated under the new Likud government from 1977. The Yom Kippur War therefore set up two contradictory legacies that the next twenty years would have to reconcile: a renewed diplomatic track that would lead to Camp David in 1978, and an entrenched occupation that would lead to the First Intifada in 1987.

Key Fact

The Yom Kippur War began on 6 October 1973 with Egyptian and Syrian attacks on Sinai and the Golan; the ceasefire under UN Resolution 338 on 22 October reactivated the land for peace principle of Resolution 242 and made the diplomacy of the late 1970s possible.

Some students reduce the Yom Kippur War to who won militarily and conclude that Israel did. The political picture is more interesting and is what examiners reward. Sadat’s aim was never to recover Sinai by force; it was to shock the Israeli public out of its post-1967 confidence, restore Egyptian honour after the humiliation of 1967, and force the United States to take Egyptian negotiation seriously. All three were achieved by 22 October. The encirclement of the Egyptian Third Army in the war’s last days — lifted only by US pressure on Israel — gave Kissinger the leverage to begin shuttle diplomacy in November and produced the Sinai disengagement agreements of 1974 and 1975. The road to Camp David in 1978 began on the night of 6 October 1973.

The October 1973 Oil Shock

On 17 October 1973, eleven days into the Yom Kippur War, the Arab members of OPEC, organised as OAPEC, agreed to cut oil production by 5% a month and to embargo states that supported Israel. The United States, the Netherlands, Portugal and South Africa were named. Within three months the world price of oil quadrupled, from about $3 a barrel to $12. Petrol queues formed at American gas stations; the United Kingdom imposed a three-day working week; Western European industrial output fell. The oil embargo made the Arab-Israeli conflict, for the first time, a problem the entire world economy could feel.

Key Fact

OAPEC began its production cuts and embargo on 17 October 1973. World oil prices quadrupled within three months. Western recession, petrol queues in the United States and Britain’s three-day week followed, making US administrations far more willing to pressure Israel into negotiations.

Kissinger and Shuttle Diplomacy

US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger had brokered the ceasefire that ended the Yom Kippur War on 25 October 1973. Over the next twenty months he flew repeatedly between Jerusalem, Cairo and Damascus to negotiate disengagement deals between the armies that had stopped fighting but not gone home. The press named the practice shuttle diplomacy. Sinai Disengagement I (January 1974) pulled Israeli and Egyptian forces apart along the canal. Sinai Disengagement II (September 1975) handed back the western Sinai oilfields and created a buffer zone monitored by US technicians. The Suez Canal, blocked since 1967, reopened to international shipping in June 1975. Kissinger had not produced peace, but he had produced motion — and motion was new.

Some students treat the United States and the Soviet Union as background to a regional conflict. The 1973–79 sequence shows the opposite. The oil embargo worked because Western dependence on Saudi crude had been built up during the Cold War oil boom. Sadat’s decision to expel his Soviet advisers in 1972 and pivot to the United States made an Egyptian-American relationship possible by 1977. Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy could only function because Egypt accepted, for the first time, that Washington and not Moscow held the keys to the Sinai. The Cold War was the road that led to Camp David, not the weather around it.

Sadat in Jerusalem, November 1977

On 9 November 1977 Egyptian President Anwar Sadat told his parliament that he was willing to go to the Israeli Knesset to negotiate. Many at home and abroad assumed it was a rhetorical flourish. Ten days later he flew to Tel Aviv. He addressed the Knesset on 20 November and offered Israel full peace, full recognition and open borders in return for withdrawal from Sinai and a settlement of the Palestinian issue. No Arab head of state had ever visited Israel. Three Egyptian ministers resigned in protest; Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Libya denounced the visit; Syria broke relations with Egypt. Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin made a reciprocal visit to Ismailia in Egypt on 25 December 1977. The two leaders had agreed nothing concrete — but the taboo on direct dealings had been broken.

Camp David, September 1978

Negotiations stalled for nine months until US President Jimmy Carter invited Sadat and Begin to the presidential retreat in Maryland. The thirteen-day summit at Camp David began on 5 September 1978. Carter shuttled between Sadat’s and Begin’s cabins because the two leaders refused to share a room after the third day. On 17 September the three signed two framework documents in the White House. The first set out an Egypt-Israel peace based on full Israeli withdrawal from Sinai. The second proposed Palestinian ‘autonomy’ in the West Bank and Gaza, with a five-year transition. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize. Carter’s mediation salvaged a deal his advisers had told him was already lost.

Key Fact

Sadat addressed the Israeli Knesset on 20 November 1977. The Camp David Accords were signed on 17 September 1978: a framework for Egypt-Israel peace and a separate framework for Palestinian autonomy. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize.

The Treaty of Washington, March 1979

On 26 March 1979 Sadat and Begin signed the Treaty of Washington on the South Lawn of the White House. Egypt became the first Arab state to recognise Israel. Israel committed to phased withdrawal from Sinai by 1982 and to dismantling its settlements there. The Suez Canal was opened to Israeli shipping. Full diplomatic relations followed in February 1980. Egypt received around $1.3 billion a year in US military aid; Israel received around $3 billion. The treaty held: every Israeli soldier and settler had left Sinai by April 1982, on schedule.

Arab Reaction and the Cost

The Arab League suspended Egypt at a Baghdad summit in March 1979 and moved its headquarters from Cairo to Tunis; only Oman, Sudan and Somalia kept full relations with Egypt. The Palestinian autonomy track, which had no Palestinian or Jordanian negotiators, produced nothing — King Hussein refused to be drawn in and the PLO rejected a deal made over Palestinian heads. On 6 October 1981, while reviewing a Cairo military parade marking the 1973 war, Sadat was assassinated by Egyptian Islamist soldiers who regarded the treaty as a betrayal. He was succeeded by Hosni Mubarak, who upheld the treaty for the next thirty years. Egypt was readmitted to the Arab League in 1989; the headquarters returned to Cairo in 1990.

A common student claim is that 1970s peacemaking ‘failed’. The strongest answers separate two tracks. The Egypt-Israel bilateral track succeeded: the treaty was signed, Sinai was returned, the border has been quiet since. The Palestinian track failed: no Palestinians sat at Camp David, the autonomy framework was rejected by the PLO and went nowhere, and the deal arguably let Israel concentrate on the West Bank and Gaza without an Egyptian counter-weight. Examiners reward students who show that peacemaking and the wider conflict can run on separate clocks.

Why It Mattered for the 1980s

The 1979 treaty removed the largest Arab army from any future war with Israel. Without Egypt, Syria alone could not realistically open a southern front. Israel was free to invade Lebanon in 1982 in pursuit of the PLO without fearing a two-front war — the next lesson’s subject. Inside Egypt, the treaty bought economic recovery: US aid, the reopened Sinai oilfields and the canal tolls underwrote Mubarak’s long presidency. For the United States, the deal locked Egypt into the Western camp and gave the Carter administration its single foreign-policy success in a presidency otherwise defined by the Iranian hostage crisis. The cost was paid by Sadat himself, by Egypt’s standing in the Arab world for a decade, and by Palestinians whose autonomy framework was never implemented.

before.content_html:
Rabat 1974 — A Diplomatic Coronation

In October 1974, twenty Arab heads of state met at Rabat and declared the Palestine Liberation Organisation, led by Yasser Arafat, the ‘sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people’. The Rabat resolution mattered because it stripped King Hussein of Jordan of his long-standing claim to speak for the Palestinians of the West Bank, lost to Israel in 1967. From now on, any Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank would have to be negotiated with the PLO. A month later, on 13 November 1974, Arafat addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, his pistol holster prominent on his belt. ‘Today I have come bearing an olive branch and a freedom-fighter’s gun’, he said. ‘Do not let the olive branch fall from my hand.’ The assembly granted the PLO permanent observer status. For one year, the Palestinian cause looked diplomatically unstoppable.

Key Fact

At Rabat in October 1974 the Arab League declared the PLO the ‘sole legitimate representative’ of the Palestinians, ending King Hussein’s claim. On 13 November 1974 Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly with the ‘gun and olive branch’ speech, and the PLO was granted permanent observer status.

The PLO Mini-State in Lebanon

After King Hussein expelled the PLO from Jordan in 1970–71, the leadership relocated to Lebanon, taking advantage of the 1969 Cairo Agreement that allowed armed Palestinian operations from Lebanese soil. By the mid-1970s the PLO ran what observers called ‘Fatahland’ in southern Lebanon — armed checkpoints, social services, courts, schools. In April 1975 a sectarian massacre on a Palestinian bus in Beirut helped touch off the Lebanese civil war. The Palestinians, mostly Sunni, fought alongside Lebanese leftist and Druze militias against the Maronite Christian Phalange. Syria intervened in 1976 with around 20,000 troops, switching sides as the conflict shifted. Lebanon ceased to function as a state, and the PLO acquired the freedom of action it had lost in Jordan.

Reprisals, the Litani Operation and UNIFIL

PLO rocket and cross-border raids drew Israeli reprisals throughout the 1970s. After a Fatah coastal raid killed thirty-eight Israelis on the Tel Aviv road in March 1978, Prime Minister Begin sent the IDF into southern Lebanon. The operation pushed PLO forces north of the Litani river and left a Christian-led Israeli proxy force, the ‘South Lebanon Army’, in control of a six-mile buffer zone. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 425 calling for Israeli withdrawal and authorised UNIFIL, the UN peacekeeping force still on the border today. The Israeli army withdrew — partially — but reprisals and rockets continued.

It is tempting to treat ‘the PLO’ and ‘the Palestinians’ as one block, but the spec rewards students who keep them distinct. The PLO was an umbrella body led by Arafat’s Fatah, but it also contained the Marxist-Leninist PFLP and other smaller factions, each with its own line. After Rabat 1974 the PLO was the diplomatic representative of the Palestinians, but it was an Arab-state-funded leadership living in Lebanon, not a government chosen by Palestinians on the West Bank or in Gaza. By 1987, when the Intifada broke out spontaneously among occupied Palestinians, the PLO leadership in Tunis was caught off guard. The collapse of the PLO’s Lebanese position in 1982, the topic of this lesson, set up that disconnect directly.

Operation Peace for Galilee, June 1982

On 3 June 1982 Palestinian gunmen of the Abu Nidal faction shot the Israeli ambassador to London, Shlomo Argov. Begin’s cabinet, with Defence Minister Ariel Sharon driving the planning, used the attack as the trigger for an invasion that had been prepared for months. Operation Peace for Galilee began on 6 June 1982. Sharon promised the cabinet a forty-kilometre advance to remove PLO artillery from northern Israel; in practice the IDF drove on to Beirut and besieged the western half of the city for ten weeks. An estimated 17,000 Lebanese and Palestinian civilians and combatants were killed during the 1982 invasion and siege. US envoy Philip Habib brokered an evacuation deal in August 1982: PLO fighters and headquarters staff would leave Lebanon under multinational supervision and disperse to eight Arab countries. About 14,000 PLO personnel left by ship; Arafat and his Fatah staff went to Tunis, more than 1,500 miles from any Palestinian territory.

Sabra and Shatila, September 1982

On 14 September 1982 the Christian Phalange leader and Lebanese President-elect Bashir Gemayel was assassinated. The IDF moved into West Beirut and let Phalange militias enter the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps to flush out remaining PLO fighters. Between the night of 16 September and the morning of 18 September the militiamen massacred between 700 and 3,500 unarmed Palestinian civilians. The IDF, which had ringed the camps with flares to light the area for the killers, did not intervene. The Israeli government’s own Kahan Commission reported in February 1983 that Israel bore ‘indirect responsibility’; Sharon was forced to resign as Defence Minister, though he remained in cabinet. About 400,000 Israelis — one in ten of the population — demonstrated against the war in Tel Aviv on 25 September 1982, the largest protest in Israel’s history.

Key Fact

Operation Peace for Galilee began on 6 June 1982. After a ten-week siege of Beirut the PLO leadership was evacuated to Tunis in August 1982. The Kahan Commission reported in February 1983 that Israel bore ‘indirect responsibility’ for the Sabra and Shatila massacre; Sharon resigned as Defence Minister.

Hezbollah and the New Map of Resistance

The 1982 invasion did not end Israel’s problem in Lebanon — it changed it. Iran sent Revolutionary Guards to the Bekaa Valley to organise Lebanon’s long-marginalised Shia community. The new movement, Hezbollah, used suicide truck bombs against the IDF, the multinational force and the US embassy. The October 1983 bombings of the US Marine and French paratrooper barracks killed 241 American and 58 French troops in a single morning. The multinational force withdrew. Israel pulled back to the south Lebanon ‘security zone’ in 1985 but stayed there until 2000. The PLO had been displaced as the symbol of armed resistance to Israel by a Shia movement Israel had not anticipated.

A common shorthand is that Israel won militarily in 1982 but lost politically. Examiner indicative content for the 2023 importance prompt rewards more granularity. The PLO had its mini-state, headquarters and roughly 14,000 fighters removed from a country bordering Israel. Arafat, in distant Tunis, was harder to reach but also harder to lead from. The vacuum was filled by Hezbollah and, on the West Bank itself by 1987, by Hamas, both of which rejected the PLO’s eventual two-state turn. Sabra and Shatila, the protests in Tel Aviv and the Kahan Commission marked the first sustained Israeli internal challenge to a war policy. The PLO was militarily defeated, diplomatically isolated in Tunis, and yet politically more central than ever — because no replacement representative existed. That contradiction set up the next two years.

The PLO Reset

From 1983 to 1987 the PLO leadership in Tunis tried to reach the Palestinians it could no longer touch directly. Arafat survived a Syrian-backed Fatah mutiny in 1983 and an Israeli air strike on his Tunis headquarters in October 1985. The Palestinian National Council in Algiers in 1987 began drafting language that would lead, in November 1988, to the formal renunciation of terrorism — the topic of the next lesson. By the time the Intifada began in December 1987, the PLO leadership was a distant authority that the children of Gaza throwing stones recognised only as a flag and a name. Lebanon had given the PLO a base; it had also stripped it down to the point where it would have to make compromises a stronger PLO would never have considered.
